title: Company Accounts: Accounting for Share Capital
description: Class 12 Accountancy: company and kinds of share capital, issue of shares at par and premium, calls, over-subscription, calls-in-arrears and calls-in-advance, and forfeiture and re-issue of shares.

topics.title: Company, Shares and Kinds of Share Capital
topics.concept:
A company is a voluntary association of persons, incorporated under the Companies Act, with a separate legal entity, perpetual succession, a common seal and limited liability for its members. Its capital is divided into units of small denomination called shares; a person holding shares is a shareholder.

Shares are of two kinds:

  • Preference shares — carry a preferential right to a fixed dividend and to repayment of capital on winding up, before equity shares.
  • Equity shares — the ordinary shares; they get dividends after preference shares, carry voting rights, and bear the main risk and reward.

The term share capital is used at several levels, which the exam loves to test:

TermMeaning
Authorised (Nominal) capitalthe maximum capital the company is allowed to raise (stated in the Memorandum).
Issued capitalthe part of authorised capital actually offered to the public.
Subscribed capitalthe part of issued capital actually applied for by the public.
Called-up capitalthe part of subscribed capital the company has asked shareholders to pay.
Paid-up capitalthe amount actually received against the called-up capital.

So Authorised ≥ Issued ≥ Subscribed ≥ Called-up ≥ Paid-up. Understanding these layers is essential before recording the issue of shares.

examples.problem: Example 1: State two features of a company.
examples.solution:
Distinct legal traits.

  • Separate legal entity and limited liability (also perpetual succession, common seal).
examples.answer: Separate legal entity and limited liability (others: perpetual succession, common seal).

examples.problem: Example 2: Which shares get a fixed dividend before others?
examples.solution:
Preference first.

  • Preference shares carry a preferential right to a fixed dividend.

examples.problem: Example 3: The maximum capital a company may raise is its ____ capital.
examples.solution:
The cap.

  • Authorised (nominal) capital, stated in the Memorandum.

recap:
• Company: separate legal entity, perpetual succession, limited liability, common seal; capital in shares.
  • Preference shares (fixed dividend first) vs equity shares (ordinary, voting, residual).
  • Capital layers: Authorised ≥ Issued ≥ Subscribed ≥ Called-up ≥ Paid-up.

quiz.q: The maximum capital a company is allowed to raise is its:
quiz.explanation: Authorised (nominal) capital is the maximum, stated in the Memorandum.

quiz.q: Shares with a preferential right to a fixed dividend are:
quiz.explanation: Preference shares carry a fixed, prior dividend.

topics.title: Issue of Shares: Par, Premium, and Calls
topics.concept:
A company collects the price of a share in instalments: application, allotment, and one or more calls (first call, second/final call). Each instalment is recorded when the money is due and again when received.

If shares are issued at par (at face value), the entries for, say, a Rs 10 share collected as Rs 3 on application, Rs 4 on allotment and Rs 3 on first & final call are:

  • On application: Bank A/c Dr / To Share Application A/c.
  • On allotment due: Share Application A/c Dr (transfer) and Share Allotment A/c Dr / To Share Capital A/c.
  • On allotment received: Bank A/c Dr / To Share Allotment A/c.
  • On call: Share Call A/c Dr / To Share Capital A/c; then Bank A/c Dr / To Share Call A/c.

Issue at premium. When a share is issued for more than its face value, the excess is the securities premium. It is credited to the Securities Premium Reserve A/c (a capital reserve), never to Share Capital. For a Rs 10 share issued at Rs 12 (premium Rs 2, usually with allotment): Share Allotment A/c Dr / To Share Capital A/c and To Securities Premium Reserve A/c. The premium can be used only for specified purposes under Section 52 — issuing bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, premium on redemption, or buy-back. Note that issuing shares at a discount is generally prohibited (Section 53), except sweat equity. So the two real cases are at par and at premium.

examples.problem: Example 1: A Rs 10 share is issued at Rs 13. What is the premium and where is it credited?
examples.solution:
Excess over face value.

  • Premium = 13 − 10 = 3.
  • Credited to Securities Premium Reserve A/c.
examples.answer: Premium Rs 3 per share, credited to the Securities Premium Reserve Account.

examples.problem: Example 2: What entry records money received on application?
examples.solution:
Bank in.

  • Bank A/c Dr / To Share Application A/c.
examples.answer: Bank A/c Dr; To Share Application A/c.

examples.problem: Example 3: Can shares normally be issued at a discount?
examples.solution:
Generally no.

  • Section 53 prohibits issuing shares at a discount (except sweat equity).
examples.answer: No — issuing shares at a discount is generally prohibited (except sweat equity shares).

recap:
• Share price is collected in instalments: application → allotment → call(s); each recorded when due and when received.
  • Premium (excess over face value) → Securities Premium Reserve A/c (never Share Capital); used only for Section 52 purposes.
  • Issue at a discount is prohibited (Sec 53), except sweat equity.

quiz.q: The amount received over the face value of a share is the:
quiz.explanation: The excess over face value is the securities premium.

quiz.q: Securities premium is credited to the Securities Premium Reserve A/c, not to:
quiz.explanation: Premium is kept separate from Share Capital.

topics.title: Over-subscription, Calls-in-Arrears, Calls-in-Advance and Forfeiture
topics.concept:
A popular issue may be over-subscribed — more shares applied for than offered. The company cannot allot more than it issued, so it deals with the excess by: rejecting some applications (refund money), making a pro-rata allotment (allot proportionately and adjust excess application money towards allotment), or a combination.

Two timing issues on calls:

  • Calls-in-Arrears — an amount called but not yet paid by a shareholder. It is shown as a deduction from called-up capital; interest may be charged (up to 10% p.a. per Table F).
  • Calls-in-Advance — an amount paid before it is called. It is a liability of the company; interest may be paid (up to 12% p.a. per Table F).

Forfeiture of shares. If a shareholder fails to pay the calls, the company may forfeit (cancel) his shares after due notice. On forfeiture, the Share Capital account is debited with the called-up amount, the amount already received is transferred to a Forfeited Shares A/c (a capital reserve in the making), and the unpaid calls are cancelled. The forfeited shares can then be re-issued, usually at a discount not exceeding the amount forfeited. On re-issue, the loss (discount allowed) is met from the Forfeited Shares A/c, and any balance left in it is transferred to Capital Reserve.

For example, if Rs 5 had been received on a Rs 10 forfeited share later re-issued at Rs 8 (discount Rs 2), the Rs 2 discount is taken from the Rs 5 forfeited amount, and the remaining Rs 3 goes to Capital Reserve. These adjustments complete the accounting for share capital from issue to re-issue.

examples.solution:
More applied than offered.

  • When applications received exceed the number of shares issued.
examples.answer: When the public applies for more shares than the company has issued.

examples.solution:
Unpaid vs prepaid.

  • Calls-in-arrears: called but not yet paid (deducted from capital).
  • Calls-in-advance: paid before being called (a liability).
examples.answer: Calls-in-arrears = called but unpaid (deducted from capital); calls-in-advance = paid before being called (a liability).

examples.problem: Example 3: Rs 4 was received on a Rs 10 forfeited share, re-issued at Rs 9. How much goes to Capital Reserve?
examples.solution:
Forfeited less re-issue discount.

  • Discount on re-issue = 10 − 9 = 1.
  • Capital Reserve = 4 − 1 = 3.
examples.answer: Rs 3 is transferred to Capital Reserve (Rs 4 forfeited less Rs 1 re-issue discount).

recap:
• Over-subscription: reject / pro-rata allotment / adjust excess money to allotment.
  • Calls-in-arrears (unpaid, deducted from capital, interest up to 10% p.a.); calls-in-advance (prepaid, a liability, interest up to 12% p.a.).
  • Forfeiture: cancel shares, keep received amount in Forfeited Shares A/c; on re-issue, cover the discount, transfer the balance to Capital Reserve.

quiz.q: An amount called but not yet paid by a shareholder is:
quiz.explanation: Calls-in-arrears is the unpaid called amount.

quiz.q: On re-issue of forfeited shares, the balance of the Forfeited Shares A/c is transferred to:
quiz.explanation: Any balance left after meeting the re-issue discount goes to Capital Reserve.

questions.q: A company has a separate ____ from its members.
questions.explanation: A company is a separate legal entity.

questions.q: Shares with a fixed dividend paid before equity shares are:
questions.explanation: Preference shares get a fixed dividend first.

questions.q: The maximum capital a company can raise is its ____ capital.
questions.explanation: Authorised (nominal) capital is the maximum.

questions.q: The part of issued capital applied for by the public is ____ capital.
questions.explanation: Subscribed capital is what the public applies for.

questions.q: The amount actually received against called-up capital is ____ capital.
questions.explanation: Paid-up capital is the amount received.

questions.q: The excess of issue price over face value is the:
questions.explanation: The excess is the securities premium.

questions.q: Securities premium is credited to:
questions.explanation: It goes to the Securities Premium Reserve A/c.

questions.q: Money received on application is recorded as:
options: Bank A/c Dr; To Share Application A/c
Share Application A/c Dr; To Bank
questions.explanation: Bank is debited; Share Application credited.

questions.q: Issuing shares at a discount is generally:
questions.explanation: Section 53 prohibits it except sweat equity.

questions.q: More applications than shares issued is called:
questions.explanation: Over-subscription = applications exceed shares offered.

questions.q: An amount called but unpaid is:
questions.explanation: Unpaid called amount = calls-in-arrears.

questions.q: An amount paid before being called is:
questions.explanation: Prepaid call = calls-in-advance (a liability).

questions.q: Cancelling shares for non-payment of calls is:
questions.explanation: Forfeiture cancels the defaulter's shares.

questions.q: On re-issue, the balance of the Forfeited Shares A/c goes to:
questions.explanation: Any balance left is transferred to Capital Reserve.

questions.q: Rs 6 received on a Rs 10 forfeited share, re-issued at Rs 8. Capital Reserve =
questions.explanation: Forfeited 6 − re-issue discount 2 = 4 to Capital Reserve.

questions.q: A company issues 10,000 shares but receives applications for 15,000 and makes a pro-rata allotment to all. The excess application money is:
questions.explanation: In a pro-rata allotment the surplus application money is carried forward to adjust against allotment (and later calls).

questions.q: A Rs 10 share (premium Rs 2 on allotment) is forfeited after the holder paid application Rs 3 only; allotment Rs 6 (incl. premium) unpaid. On forfeiture, Securities Premium Reserve is:
options: Debited (cancelled), as the premium was never received
questions.explanation: Premium not yet received must be reversed/cancelled on forfeiture; only premium actually received stays credited.

questions.q: 1,000 shares of Rs 10 are forfeited after Rs 5 per share had been received; they are re-issued as fully paid for Rs 7 each. The Capital Reserve created is:
questions.explanation: Forfeited amount Rs 5,000 (5 × 1,000); re-issue discount = (10 − 7) × 1,000 = Rs 3,000; Capital Reserve = 5,000 − 3,000 = Rs 2,000.

questions.q: Why is securities premium NOT available for paying ordinary cash dividends?
options: It is a capital receipt restricted by Section 52 to specified uses
questions.explanation: Premium is a capital reserve usable only for the purposes listed in Section 52, not for distributing dividends.

questions.q: Calls-in-advance, under Table F, may carry interest payable by the company up to:
questions.explanation: The company may pay up to 12% p.a. on calls-in-advance (and charge up to 10% on calls-in-arrears).

questions.q: On forfeiture of shares originally issued at par, the Share Capital Account is debited with the:
options: Called-up amount per share × number forfeited
questions.explanation: Share Capital is debited with the called-up value of the forfeited shares; amount received is moved to Forfeited Shares A/c.

questions.q: Authorised, issued, subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital are related as:
questions.explanation: Each layer is a subset of the one before it.

questions.q: A shareholder holding 100 shares (Rs 10, Rs 7 called) has not paid the Rs 3 first call. Calls-in-arrears shown is:
questions.explanation: Unpaid call = 100 × Rs 3 = Rs 300, deducted from called-up capital.

questions.q: Maximum a company can normally allot is its:
questions.explanation: It cannot allot more shares than it issued, however many apply.

questions.q: The Forfeited Shares Account balance before re-issue represents:
options: Money already received on the forfeited shares, held in suspense
questions.explanation: It holds the amount the company kept from the defaulting holder, pending re-issue adjustments.
